title: Allegory as lossy encoding
summary: Why private allegory exists: teach from a real situation without publishing the people inside it.

blocks.title: Allegory as lossy encoding
blocks.body: Sometimes you need to teach from a real situation — a workplace mess, a family pattern, a near-miss — without publishing the people inside it. Allegory is not decoration. Done well, it is a deliberate, lossy encoding: enough structure for a thoughtful reader to learn, not enough bits for a stranger (or a neighbor) to re-identify who you meant.

blocks.heading: Why encode at all?
blocks.body:
Plain disclosure is honest and often wrong for the medium. Names, dates, and unique combinations of facts travel farther than the conversation that justified them. Silence protects privacy but teaches nothing. Allegory sits between those poles: you keep the relationships, incentives, and failure modes that made the situation worth telling, and you discard the identifiers that only matter to the people who already lived it.

The craft is privacy engineering dressed as storytelling. This section is the map — eight rules, two checks, an underside limit, then how to practice the craft, how to use it in public, and how to treat it as art.

blocks.quote: Map the shape of the trouble, not the passport numbers of the people inside it.

columns.name: Raw disclosure
columns.detail: Names, employer, timeline, and a unique stack of quasi-identifiers. A reader who already knows the cast can confirm; a reader who does not can still search their way there.

columns.name: Allegory encoding
columns.detail: Roles, pressures, and decisions under a lossy vocabulary. A reader who lived something similar recognizes the pattern. A stranger cannot invert the story back to a shortlist of real people.

nodes.title: Lived situation
nodes.detail: People, places, dates, and stakes you are not free to publish.

nodes.title: Encode (lossy)
nodes.detail: Keep relationships and dynamics. Drop invertibility. Coarsen the rest.

nodes.title: Shared page
nodes.detail: A story that teaches. The reader's own life is the key — not a table in the appendix.

blocks.heading: How this section is organized
items: Rules 1–2: relationships over entities; lossy vocabulary on purpose.
Rules 7–8: gate on action; the reader's life as the key.
Two tests and the underside rule (encoding ≠ permission).
Society: norms for publishing allegorical encodings in public.
Art: metaphor domains and aesthetic choices that stay lossy.

blocks.title: Outside the grading night
blocks.body: This section is education for anyone writing private allegory. It is not a grading-night subject and does not sit in the gn-100 handoffs.
